subject: political-science
readings: OD ch. 6 (Orvis & Drogus, *Institutions of Participation and Representation*)

cards.front: **Hanna Pitkin** (*The Concept of Representation*, 1967) distinguishes **four senses of representation**. Name and gloss all four.
cards.back:
**① Formalistic** — the institutional arrangement that **authorises** a representative and holds them **accountable** (elections = the "before" and "after").
**② Descriptive** — the rep **resembles** the represented (gender, ethnicity, class) — *"standing for"*; the case for **quotas**.
**③ Symbolic** — the rep **stands for** the represented symbolically (a leader/flag people identify with).
**④ Substantive** — the rep **acts in the interests** of the represented — *"acting for"*.

*Why it leads:* electoral systems are really machines for producing **one kind of representation or another**.
cards.hint: Authorise · resemble · symbolise · act-for.

cards.front: Name Pitkin's sense of representation for each: (a) a legislature that **looks like** the population it serves; (b) a monarch/flag people **identify with**; (c) elections that **authorise and hold accountable**; (d) an MP who **acts in your interests**.
cards.back:
(a) **Descriptive** — *"standing for"* (the quota argument).
(b) **Symbolic**.
(c) **Formalistic**.
(d) **Substantive** — *"acting for"*.

The pairing to remember: **descriptive = standing for · substantive = acting for.**
cards.hint: Looks like · identify with · authorise · act for.

cards.front: Within Pitkin's **substantive** representation, contrast the **delegate** vs the **trustee** model of a representative.
cards.back:
**Delegate** — the rep **follows instructions**, mirroring constituents' expressed wishes.
**Trustee** — the rep uses **their own judgment** of the constituents' best interests.

Both are *"acting for"* (substantive), but they answer differently: *do you transmit the mandate, or exercise discretion?*
cards.hint: Follow the mandate vs use your own judgment.

cards.front: **PR systems elect far more women and minorities; SMD emphasises the local voter–rep link.** Map each electoral family onto the **Pitkin** sense of representation it maximises.
cards.back:
**PR → boosts *descriptive* representation** (party lists + quotas seat more women/minorities).
**SMD → emphasises the *formalistic* local link** (one identifiable district representative you authorise and can vote out).

So the choice of electoral system is implicitly a choice about *which kind of representation matters most*.
cards.hint: Lists & quotas vs one local name on the ballot.

cards.front: **Why is voting individually "irrational," and how do institutions get people to the polls anyway?** Run the logic.
cards.back:
**Downs (1957):** one vote almost never decides the outcome, so voting is technically **irrational** → participation is a **collective-action problem** (all suffer if none act).

**People vote anyway** for **expressive/solidaristic** reasons, charismatic leaders, and to avoid the **emotional cost** of not voting (guilt, exclusion).

**Institutions shape turnout:** complex systems depress it among the less-educated; **PR/mixed systems raise it** (fewer *wasted votes*); parties & interest groups lower the cost of finding and acting on your interests.
cards.hint: Downs → collective action → institutions raise/lower the cost.

cards.front: List the **electoral-system menu** — the four families a democracy can choose from.
cards.back:
**① SMD plurality (FPTP)** — most votes in each single-member district wins, no majority needed.
**② Majoritarian** — winner needs an **absolute majority (50%+1)**: two-round runoff or Alternative Vote.
**③ Proportional (PR)** — seats **= vote share** (large districts/national, usually a **threshold**).
**④ Mixed / semiproportional** — SMD seats **+** a party-list PR tier.

The electoral system is the **master lever**: it sets *on what basis you're represented* (district · party/idea · group) and *how votes become seats*.
cards.hint: FPTP · majoritarian · PR · mixed.

cards.front: **Which electoral system?** (a) most votes in a district wins, no majority needed; (b) seats equal vote share with a threshold; (c) rank candidates, eliminate the last-placed and transfer votes until one clears 50%; (d) a district ballot *plus* a party-list ballot.
cards.back:
(a) **SMD plurality / FPTP**.
(b) **Proportional representation (PR)**.
(c) **Alternative Vote (AV) / ranked-choice / instant-runoff** (a majoritarian type).
(d) **Mixed / semiproportional**.
cards.hint: FPTP · PR · AV · mixed.

cards.front: **This feature → which system?** (a) *wasted votes & extreme disproportionality*; (b) *coalition instability & outsized leverage for small parties*; (c) *strong single-party government + clear accountability*; (d) *best representation of women & minorities*.
cards.back:
(a) **SMD/FPTP** (a party can win big on ~35% pluralities; broad-but-thin parties win almost nothing).
(b) **PR**.
(c) **SMD/FPTP** (the flip side of (a)).
(d) **PR**.

This is the **Powell trade-off** in miniature: (c) vs (b)/(d) are two ends of the same line.
cards.hint: Wasted votes · instability · single-party rule · women/minorities.

cards.front: **Alternative Vote (AV / ranked-choice): three candidates — A 40%, B 35%, C 25%, nobody at 50%.** Walk the count to the winner.
cards.back:
One ballot, but voters **rank** 1-2-3. Count 1st preferences; if nobody has 50%+1, **eliminate the last-placed candidate and transfer their ballots to each voter's next choice**; repeat until someone passes 50%.

Here: eliminate **C**; C's 2nd choices split (say **+18%→B, +7%→A**). New totals: **A 47% · B 53% → B wins** — even though **A led the first count**.

*The point:* it rewards the **broadly acceptable** candidate over the one with the biggest *minority*. (Case: **Maine 2018** — Golden won **50.5–49.5 after trailing** on the first count, first US Congress seat by AV.)
cards.hint: Eliminate last, transfer, repeat until 50%.

cards.front: Both are **majoritarian** (need 50%+1). Distinguish the **two-round system (runoff)** from the **Alternative Vote (AV)**.
cards.back:
**Two-round system (TRS) — *France.*** Round 1: win outright with 50%+1; if not, the top candidates (top two, or in France's legislative version *everyone above 12.5% of registered voters*) go to a **second-round runoff** a week or two later. Voters whose first choice is out get to **re-choose**.

**Alternative Vote (AV) — *one ballot.*** You **rank** candidates; eliminate the last-placed and transfer votes **instantly** until one passes 50% — a runoff done in a single election.

*Both* squeeze extremes and reward second-choice-friendly candidates → **~two blocs**, but more softly than FPTP.
cards.hint: Two separate elections vs one instant runoff.

cards.front: Under PR you fill a party's seats from a candidate **list**. Contrast **closed-list** vs **open-list** — *who decides the order?*
cards.back:
**Closed list** — the **party** fixes the order in advance; you vote only for the party, and its *n* won seats go to the top *n* names. → **more party control, discipline, and easy quotas** (guarantee women high spots), but no voter choice of individual. *(Israel.)*

**Open list** — you vote for the party **and** a **specific candidate**; the candidates' *own* vote totals decide who is seated. → **more voter choice**, but candidates compete against party-mates → **weaker, more personalist parties**. *(Brazil — a big reason its parties are fragmented and weak.)*
cards.hint: Party sets the rank vs voters set the rank.

cards.front: In **mixed** systems, contrast Germany's **compensatory** version with Japan's **noncompensatory** version.
cards.back:
Both give two ballots — a **district candidate** + a **party list** — blending a personal rep with proportional fairness.

**Compensatory (Germany):** the list tier **tops seats up to full proportionality** → highly proportional, sustains a multiparty system.
**Noncompensatory (Japan):** SMD and PR tiers are kept **separate** → **less proportional**, more majoritarian.

*Note:* Germany's **2023 reform** (first used 2025) **capped the Bundestag at 630** and **scrapped overhang/compensatory seats** — seats now follow the **list vote**, and a district win no longer guarantees a seat (*Zweitstimmendeckung*), so many now call it **"personalised PR"** rather than truly mixed.
cards.hint: Top-up to proportional vs keep the tiers separate.

cards.front: **Duverger's Law:** state it, then explain the *two mechanisms* by which **SMD → two parties**.
cards.back:
**Duverger's Law: SMD/plurality → two parties; PR → multiparty.**

Under **SMD** you must come **first in a district** to win *anything*, so:
**① Mechanical effect** — small/ideological parties get **no seats** and wither.
**② Psychological effect** — voters **stop "wasting" votes** on no-hopers and defect to viable ones.

Both pressures collapse politics toward **two broad catch-all parties**. Under **PR** (seats ≈ vote share) *both* pressures vanish → **multiparty survives**.
cards.hint: Mechanical (no seats) + psychological (no wasted votes).

cards.front: **FPTP "should" give two parties, yet India runs a national multiparty system, and France's two-bloc system collapsed in 2017.** What do these show about Duverger's Law?
cards.back:
**Duverger's Law is not deterministic — it holds in *established* democracies, not new/diverse ones.**

**India:** huge **diversity + federalism** → many *state-level* two-party fights aggregate into a **national multiparty** system; voters aren't strategic (ethnic/identity voting persists), so FPTP winners take seats on 20–30% (**Moser & Scheiner**; Boix).

**France 2017:** the classic Duverger case (two-round SMD had pushed the top two to **82% of seats by 2012**) — until **Macron's one-year-old party blew it up**. Even old systems can break.
cards.hint: Established vs new/diverse; France's 2017 shock.

cards.front: Parties perform **five functions** (FK deck) — and one feature separates them from interest groups. Name all five plus the distinction.
cards.back:
**① Mobilise** citizens to participate · **② recruit** the political elite (candidates/leaders) · **③ simplify** choices (a label voters can reason with) · **④ organise government** (form and run the executive/legislature) · **⑤ provide opposition** (a government-in-waiting that scrutinises).

**The distinction:** **parties seek office**; **interest groups only seek influence**.
cards.hint: Mobilise · recruit · simplify · govern · oppose.

cards.front: **Which party-system type?** (a) many parties compete freely but **one wins every election**; (b) only **two** can realistically win; (c) **more than two** can win → coalitions. Give a case for each.
cards.back:
(a) **Dominant-party** — **ANC**, South Africa (won all six post-apartheid elections; share fell to **57.5% in 2019**). *Nuance:* the line to **electoral authoritarianism** is thin — test *how* it keeps winning (genuine popularity vs rigging rules/state resources/intimidation).
(b) **Two-party** — **US** (no significant third party since the 1850s Republicans; Perot's Reform Party flared and died), UK.
(c) **Multiparty** — **Italy** → coalitions.

Classify by the **number & relative strength** of parties.
cards.hint: One always wins · only two can win · >two can win.

cards.front: Two rival explanations for *why some countries have 2 parties and others 6*: the **sociological** vs the **institutional** account. Contrast them.
cards.back:
**Sociological — parties grow out of social *cleavages*.** A party forms to represent a self-conscious group, so the **number of parties mirrors the number of deep divisions**. Classic 19th-c. cleavages: **economic (capital vs labour)** — universal with industrialisation (every country got a business party + a workers' party) — and **religious** — present only in *some* (Germany's CDU/CSU for a Catholic minority; France, all-Catholic, needed none). *Rule:* each extra salient cleavage adds a party family.

**Institutional (Duverger) — the *electoral rules* shape the count.** Rational politicians build whatever wins under the given rules → **SMD → two parties; PR → multiparty**.

*Bridge:* the institutional effect holds in **established** democracies, not new ones (identity voting persists).
cards.hint: Cleavages (bottom-up) vs electoral rules (top-down).

cards.front: A party wins support by (a) **offering ideas/ideology/policy**; (b) **trading material benefits for votes via local brokers**; (c) **a personalist leader framing "the people" vs a "corrupt elite."** Name each **mobilisation type** and where it thrives.
cards.back:
(a) **Programmatic** — manifestos, left–right positioning; thrives in **established, richer democracies**. *(Caveat: **Achen & Bartels'** "folk theory" — voters mostly vote by **social identity**, so pure programmatic appeal is partly a myth.)*
(b) **Patronage / clientelist** — jobs, cash, favours, "get out the vote" machines; thrives in **poorer/newer, statist** economies.
(c) **Populist** — crisis rhetoric, anti-establishment, deliberate "**bad manners**"; thrives **anywhere in a "crisis of party democracy."**
cards.hint: Ideas · rewards · anti-elite personalism.

cards.front: Parties map onto **two ideology axes** (FK / Von Beyme, OD Fig. 6.4), not one. Name both axes and where today's far-right mobilises.
cards.back:
**Horizontal = economic Left–Right** (redistribution: *state intervention to increase equality* ⇄ *no intervention*).
**Vertical = cultural GAL–TAN** — **GAL** (Green/Alternative/Libertarian: progressive, cosmopolitan, pro-environment, individual rights) vs **TAN/TAL** (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist).

A party's position is the **pair** of coordinates: two parties can share an economic stance yet be opposites on culture. Today's populist far-right (**Farage, Salvini, AfD, RN, Fidesz**) mobilises mainly on the **TAN** end of this *second* axis.
cards.hint: Economics (horizontal) + culture GAL–TAN (vertical).

cards.front: Diagnose the **"crisis of party democracy"** — the symptoms, the two competing explanations, and the far-right's rise.
cards.back:
**Symptoms:** only ~**20%** trust parties (yet ~80% value democracy); falling loyalty/membership/turnout, rising **electoral volatility**, single-issue/postmaterialist voting, and anti-system parties.

**Dealignment vs realignment:** do voters **detach from all parties** (dealignment) or **switch** allegiances (realignment)? Plus catch-all parties → **"cartel parties" (Mair)** colluding at the centre → lost efficacy.

**Far-right rise (The PopuList):** anti-establishment vote across 31 European countries **~doubled, ~12% (1993) → ~31% (2022)**, driven mainly by **far-right populists**. **US exception:** not dealignment but partisan **sorting/polarisation (Abramowitz)** and Trump's **status-threat** populism (**Mutz 2018**).
cards.hint: Low trust · dealign vs realign · cartel parties · doubling far-right.

cards.front: Interest groups organise society in two rival models. Contrast **pluralism** vs **neocorporatism** — architecture, influence, and participation.
cards.back:
**Pluralism (US):** **many** competing groups orbit a **neutral** state; easy entry & local control, but **fragmented** clout — and **business is inherently privileged (Lindblom)**. **Schattschneider:** *"the flaw in the pluralist heaven is that the heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent"* — who *gets organised* is skewed to the well-off.

**Neocorporatism (Germany, N. Europe):** a **few large, hierarchical peak associations** the state recognises as *the* voice of each sector (peak labour, industry, employers) negotiate **binding** deals → more influence (esp. for labour countering business) but **less participatory** (little incentive to form new groups).

*Same job, opposite architecture:* **many-and-loose** vs **few-and-binding**. *(State corporatism = the mandated, authoritarian version.)*
cards.hint: Many-and-loose vs few-and-binding.

cards.front: **Is civil society declining or just changing?** Match the position to its author/title: (a) civic decline; (b) mass membership → managed advocacy; (c) activity just moved to new forms.
cards.back:
(a) **Putnam — *Bowling Alone*** — civic **decline**.
(b) **Skocpol** — mass-membership bodies gave way to **managed advocacy**.
(c) **Dalton — "Kicking in Groups"** — activity just **moved to new forms** (movements, single-issue groups).

This is the **social-capital debate**: *social capital* = networks + norms of reciprocity underpinning civil society.
cards.hint: Bowling Alone vs Kicking in Groups.

cards.front: State the **Powell trade-off** — the chapter's master finding — and which designs sit at each end.
cards.back:
**Powell trade-off: diverse representation/participation ⇄ clear accountability/governability.** *There is no free lunch — every design chooses a point on this line.*

**Open to diversity** (**PR · multiparty · pluralism**) → maximise **representation & participation**, but **blur accountability** and risk instability.
**Majoritarian** (**FPTP · two-party**) → clear accountability & single-party government, but **wasted votes** and worse representation of minorities.

The chapter's most robust empirical finding: **PR represents women far better than SMD** (Nordic **42.5%** vs US House **23.4%**; India goes further with **reserved seats**).
cards.hint: Representation ⇄ accountability; no free lunch.

cards.front: **Iversen & Soskice:** how does the *electoral system* shape not just seats but *redistribution* — and what's the empirical tell?
cards.back:
**PR → the middle class allies with the poor → bigger welfare states.**
**Majoritarian → the middle allies with the rich → smaller welfare states.**

So electoral systems shape **policy**, not just seats (the Sweden vs US welfare puzzle).

**Empirical tell (1945–98):** count years under left vs right government — under **PR the right governed only 26%** of the time; under **majoritarian, 75%**. Same democracies, opposite tilt → the electoral system **biases which side holds power over the long run**.
cards.hint: PR → middle+poor → bigger welfare; the 26% vs 75% split.

cards.front: **Which case?** (a) UKIP **12.6% → 1 seat**; (b) whole country = one district, **3.25% threshold**, three elections in 2019; (c) **open-list PR, no threshold, 30 parties** (2018); (d) FPTP + federalism, **120 of ~600 reserved seats**.
cards.back:
(a) **UK** — SMD/FPTP, two-party → **extreme disproportionality** (SNP won *fewer* votes than UKIP → **56 seats**, concentrated in Scotland).
(b) **Israel** — pure closed-list PR, hyper-multiparty → **instability under extreme diversity** (governments last ~2 years).
(c) **Brazil** — open-list PR → **weak-party fragmentation + populism** (Rousseff impeached 2016 → Bolsonaro 2018).
(d) **India** — FPTP in a diverse federation → Duverger's limits + **reserved-seat** representation (BJP 2014: **31% vote → 52% seats**).
cards.hint: UK · Israel · Brazil · India.

cards.front: **Germany and Japan both run mixed systems, yet Germany is multiparty while Japan was LDP-dominated.** Explain the divergence and what each case demonstrates.
cards.back:
**Germany — mixed *compensatory* PR + 5% threshold** (designed after Weimar). The list tier tops seats to full proportionality → a **stable multiparty system** that lets new/ideological parties in (**Greens 1983** cleared the threshold; **AfD** won its first seats in 2017 as the big two fell to **54%**). → *mixed PR sustains multiparty representation.*

**Japan — mixed *noncompensatory*** (1994 reform: 300 SMD + 180 PR, tiers kept separate) → **more majoritarian**. The **LDP dominated 1955–93** via factions & clientelism; the DPJ won **308/480 in 2009**, but the LDP swept back in 2012 ("lucky, not popular" — split opposition). → *Duverger's Law working haltingly.*
cards.hint: Compensatory top-up (Germany) vs separate tiers (Japan).

cards.front: **The reusable move for any electoral case** — state the four questions to run, then apply them to the UK.
cards.back:
For any case ask: **① which system · ② how do votes become seats · ③ how many parties result (Duverger) · ④ who gets left out — and what's traded off (representation vs accountability)?**

**UK worked:** ① **SMD/FPTP** → ② modest vote margins → big seat majorities → **single-party government** → ③ **two-party** → ④ **wasted votes & disproportionality** (UKIP 12.6% → 1 seat), fewer women/minorities — but **clear accountability**. It sits at the **accountability/governability** end of the **Powell trade-off**.
cards.hint: System → votes-to-seats → party count → who's left out.

cards.front: Tie the whole lecture together: the **chain** from participation to representation, and the two spine questions it answers.
cards.back:
**The chain: electoral system → party system → interest-group system** decides *whose interests get represented*. The **electoral system is the master lever** — **SMD/FPTP → two parties + clear accountability but wasted votes**; **PR → many parties + proportional, diverse representation but coalition instability** (Duverger).

**Two spine questions:**
**① Why participate (or not)?** — voting is individually irrational (a **collective-action problem**), so *institutions* raise or lower the cost (PR & simple systems → higher turnout).
**② Whose interests get represented?** — resolved by the chain above.

Underneath sits one unavoidable **Powell trade-off: broad representation ⇄ clear accountability** — and it all starts from **Pitkin's** prior question: *what does representation even mean?*
cards.hint: Electoral → party → interest-group; why participate + who's represented.
